title_en: Parallelizable Interior-Point ADMM for Block-Structured Nonconvex Programs
abstract_en: Physics simulation is an increasingly important computational primitive for AI, and local--global/ADMM splitting exposes its parallel structure but lacks matching finite-time convergence guarantees. We close this gap with two ADMM variants, Interior-Point ADMM (IP-ADMM), for block-structured nonconvex composite programs with smooth nonlinear inequality and affine constraints. A one-sided finite-activation wall keeps each constraint split state strictly feasible while the original-space infeasibility vanishes, giving closed-form constraint updates, one proximal call per objective block, and one equality-constrained quadratic consensus solve per iteration. \rev{To our knowledge, this makes IP-ADMM the first single-loop method that updates nonconvex inequality constraints locally and in parallel with finite-time convergence guarantees.} Ordinary IP-ADMM attains a CQ-free best-iterate weak-KKT rate of $O(K^{-1/3})$ or a banded Fritz--John rate of $O(K^{-1/4})$, which converts to KKT at $O(K^{-1/4})$ under a uniform constraint qualification; these are nearby-point certificates that reduce to conventional KKT for smooth blocks. A checkpoint variant, IP-ADMM-Ckpt, improves the asymptotic KKT exponent to $O(K^{-1/3})$. We also show how the bounds scale with the objective- and constraint-block counts and the coupling norm.

title_en: Separating learning from search and feedback in budgeted inverse design of periodic unit cells
abstract_en: To design a periodic material, engineers choose the shape and dimensions of a repeating cell to meet target properties. With few simulations, the benefit of a learned predictor can be hard to separate from the effect of which designs the search tries and how it uses simulator feedback. We compare two ways to predict properties in a library of 80 cell architectures, with up to 30 simulator calls per target. For each architecture, both searches use a table of predicted properties at different dimensions. One fills the table with predictions from neural networks. The other fits a simple model to the existing simulations for that architecture. Both searches use the difference between the predicted and simulated properties to adjust the next design. We generated 200 targets from simulated designs after fixing the analysis plan. The two searches showed no detectable difference in how often they matched all three properties within 2% or in the mean error of their returned designs. The upper limit of the 95% confidence interval for the gain in overall success rate was 4.5 percentage points. Follow-up controls on these targets changed success from 83.5% to 36.0% with a degraded table and 96.5% with an oracle table. In separate tests, using the simulation result to adjust the next design increased success for both types of table. Results cover one library and a coarse 32^3 voxel simulator. Designers can use this comparison to judge what a learned predictor adds when the search, feedback and budget are the same.

title_en: On the Applicability of $p$-adic Numbers in Computational Modules for Neural Networks
abstract_en: The applicability of $p$-adic arithmetic as an intermediate computational module in an otherwise unchanged machine-learning pipeline is investigated. A one-feature linear regression on the scikit-learn Diabetes dataset serves as the test model. The fitted coefficients are represented in $\mathbb{Q}_p$, predictions are computed in that field, and rational reconstruction is applied to the outputs. In the pyAdic experiments, rational reconstruction either returns no result or produces values that differ from the baseline predictions; changing computational precision can change both the magnitude and sign of the reconstructed value. In SageMath, forward conversions succeed, but the reconstructed predictions differ from the baseline. An alternative representation based on digit reversal fails to preserve ordinary addition because of carry propagation. Under the tested settings, none of the test predictions is reconstructed correctly. These results show that the tested conversion and reconstruction procedures do not provide a compatible intermediate module even for linear regression. title_en: Wideband Terahertz Pinching-Antenna Systems (PASS): Bandwidth Limits, Ergodic Rate, and Placement Optimization
abstract_en: Terahertz (THz) bands offer the vast bandwidth that sixth-generation (6G) networks demand, but their severe path loss makes bringing the radiator close to the user decisive. Pinching-antenna systems (PASS) do exactly this, turning path loss into a programmable parameter by sliding radiating points along a dielectric waveguide, which makes THz their native regime. That regime, however, is inherently wideband and the waveguide is dispersive, whereas every existing PASS analysis is single-frequency and assumes a non-dispersive guide. This paper develops the first wideband, dispersion-aware theory of PASS and uncovers a limitation intrinsic to the pinching mechanism. Because co-phasing by physical position equalizes path length only modulo a wavelength, a pinching array is inherently beam-squint limited, and we show its frequency response is a Dirichlet kernel with a closed-form coherence bandwidth and an irreducible dispersion floor that even true-time-delay (TTD) correction cannot remove. A single unifying law governs the behavior, in which array gain trades against both coherence bandwidth and spatial robustness through one invariant that TTD correction breaks, reaching the floor with far fewer delay elements than a conventional array. We further characterize the wideband ergodic rate under random user locations, show that molecular absorption acts as a deterministic taper that multiplies the squint, and derive a simple rule for the rate-optimal number of pinches. Finally, by exploiting the integer structure of co-phasing, we recast the non-convex placement problem as a mixed-integer program that can be solved exactly in polynomial time. Together, these results move PASS from the narrowband, dispersion-blind setting to the wideband, dispersive regime that THz operation actually requires.

title_en: A Structural Framework for Succession: Continuation, Recognition, and Realization
abstract_en: Succession asks whether an entity encountered later is the same entity that entered an arrangement earlier. For an artificial system that is fine-tuned, distilled, or copied, it has to be answered. We look for a mathematical structure weak enough to cover any such case and strong enough to support general theorems, so that results follow from the structure's conditions rather than from a particular pipeline or criterion. Succession is modeled on state/modification graphs with relational lifts that compose along paths. Within this framework we separate four questions that are often conflated: which continuations a representation admits, which descendants are compatible with a modification, which are recognized as continuing the identity, and which are realized. The framework allows one to address systematically questions of symmetry, computational complexity, recoverability, and robustness to partial realization, and we establish what the structure settles in each case before any particular criterion of identity is chosen.

title_en: Making Koopman Control Guarantees Hold on Robots
abstract_en: A Koopman controller can stabilize its learned latent-space linear model yet fail to stabilize the nonlinear plant. The learned model propagates predictions in latent space, while the deployed controller repeatedly re-encodes the measured physical state. We show that nominal closed-loop stability transfers to the nonlinear plant when the learned and true closed-loop dynamics agree to first order on the embedding's tangent space at the target. We derive a robustness margin for approximate matching and show that a stable open-loop latent model cannot exactly match an unstable equilibrium. We introduce Tangent-Invariant Koopman (TIK), which estimates a local plant linearization from offline transitions and enforces first-order matching to this estimate. TIK recovers the fitted LQR gain at the target, while a bilinear predictor captures state-dependent actuation during large maneuvers. Across four simulated unstable benchmarks, all 40 Standard Koopman controllers have stable latent closed loops, but their deployed nonlinear systems are locally unstable. In contrast, all 40 TIK controllers locally stabilize their respective nonlinear plants. An offline stability test using empirical curvature estimates identifies stable TIK controllers on two cart-pole systems, but is inconclusive under high noise. Under explicit model-error and curvature bounds, an invariant terminal set guarantees constraint satisfaction after entry under local feedback. TIK achieves 88\% constrained cart-pole swing-up success with a 0.25 ms planning budget and controls simulated seven-joint arms within 1-5 ms per step.

title_en: Shortcut Learning in Feature-Based Algorithm Selection
abstract_en: Landscape features give learning models information about the objective function for algorithm selection, algorithm configuration, and performance prediction. Should these features capture more information? Not always, because a model may rely on information that the algorithms ignore. This phenomenon is called shortcut learning, and in-distribution accuracy can hide it. We propose the Rubber Ruler Test. It transforms the objective values of test instances with random strictly increasing transformations, reruns the algorithms, and measures prediction performance. Comparison-based algorithms such as CMA-ES perform identically after the transformation, so for them any drop reveals shortcut learning. On 10-dimensional BBOB, a model for two comparison-based algorithms learned shortcuts even from normalized objective values. The R^2 of a model using all ELA features dropped from 0.85 to 0.23, below 0.45 with invariant features only. Rank-based features reduced the drop when algorithms search using ranks. Data augmentation with transformed training instances improved prediction on transformed instances for every portfolio we studied, but lowered R^2 on original instances by up to 0.31. These results suggest that models should rely only on information that the algorithms use. We recommend reporting the Rubber Ruler Test alongside in-distribution accuracy and using it to choose feature extraction and data augmentation.

title_en: On the Convergence of Continuous-Time AdamW
abstract_en: Continuous-time AdamW provides a framework for understanding whether an optimizer widely used to train large-scale neural networks settles to an equilibrium or sustains persistent motion. title_en: iEEG Can Help EEG: Improving Clinical Scalp EEG Analysis through Intracranial Priors
abstract_en: Scalp electroencephalography (EEG) is a cornerstone of clinical brain monitoring, making the quality of its signal fundamental to downstream tasks and models. However, that signal is heavily contaminated by non-neural interference and blurred by volume conduction. Existing methods operate almost exclusively within the scalp modality, so they inherit the contamination they would need to overcome. In practice, intracranial EEG (iEEG) observes the neural activity with far higher fidelity, yet it is invasive and therefore scarce, and the two modalities are rarely recorded as pairs at scale, share no common channel space, and offer no clean ground truth to directly supervise a mapping. Motivated by the neuronal synchronization mechanism shared by the two modalities, we propose a reprogramming approach that fits a signal-to-signal model on iEEG alone and freezes it as a cross-modal prior. We introduce ReBrain, a framework to transfer an iEEG-learned prior to scalp EEG, which re-expresses any scalp signal through that prior and can be inserted upstream of any downstream model with no pairing or fine-tuning. ReBrain consistently improves host models across recordings from multiple hospitals and across architecture families, and our analysis traces this gain to genuine neural structure carried by iEEG rather than to the architecture itself. This work provides evidence that a scarce clean modality can serve as a transferable prior for an abundant noisy one, offering a general recipe for cross-modal transfer among biosignals. Our code is available at https://github.com/Xianglong-Bao/ReBrain.

title_en: Fuzzy Explainable Continual Hierarchical Reinforcement Learning for Robotic Navigation
abstract_en: Continual robot navigation requires reinforcement learning policies to continuously adapt to new environments while retaining previously acquired knowledge. Experimental results on sequential multi-scenario navigation tasks demonstrate that the proposed method effectively unifies continual learning capability and policy explainability within a single reinforcement learning framework, achieving stable knowledge retention and meaningful behavioral explanation.

title_en: JointQ: Joint Scale-and-Integer Quantization for Large Language Models
abstract_en: GPTQ is the de facto standard solver for layer-wise post-training quantization (PTQ) of large language models, yet the solver itself has received less attention than weight preprocessing and cross-layer objectives. We target a bottleneck of GPTQ: its greedy procedure optimizes continuous group scales separately from the assignment of discrete integers. Evaluating each integer candidate with its closed-form optimal scale has been used for per-channel quantization; JointQ extends it to group-wise quantization, where a row's scales are coupled through the Hessian, and applies it to refine the GPTQ solution. Each local-search move changes one integer and recomputes its group's optimal scale in closed form, accounting for the other groups through the full Hessian; all scales are periodically re-solved jointly. The search starts from a row-wise selection among scale-refitted candidates including the GPTQ solution, so unregularized JointQ never has a larger layer-wise calibration error than GPTQ. JointQ preserves the GPTQ output format and is thus a drop-in replacement. Across four models and four settings, JointQ improves six-task average zero-shot accuracy over vanilla GPTQ in 14 of 16 comparisons and perplexity in 12 of 16. The mean accuracy gain increases from 0.0044 in W4G128 to 0.1559 in W3 per-channel, and JointQ also improves average accuracy over GPTQ with MSE-based scale search and activation ordering in all eight per-channel comparisons, though rarely in G128. An ablation shows that JointQ's diagonal Tikhonov regularization mitigates severe W3 per-channel perplexity degradation, so the largest gains are not due to the local search alone. Overall, JointQ's primary empirical benefit is downstream accuracy preservation in challenging low-bit and large-group regimes. title_en: Architectural Principles for Parameter-Efficient Unitary Transformations in Coherent Optical Neural Networks
abstract_en: Coherent optical neural networks based on interferometric architectures offer a promising route toward high-throughput, energy-efficient computation by exploiting the multiple degrees of freedom of light, including spatial, temporal, and spectral modes. title_en: Settling the Support Complexity of Correlated Equilibria
abstract_en: We study the support complexity of approximate correlated equilibria (CE) in two-player games, that is, the minimum number of pure action profiles that must be assigned positive probability to approximate a correlated equilibrium of a two-player matrix game. For $\varepsilon$-approximate coarse correlated equilibria, constant approximation is possible with support $O(\log N/\varepsilon^2)$ in $N\times N$ games. For correlated equilibria, the best known upper bound was $O(\log^2 N/\varepsilon^4)$ [Babichenko et al., 2014, 2017], but whether this bound was tight remained open. We establish a matching lower bound, resolving the open question of Ko and Schvartzman [2017]. Specifically, we show that, already for two-player zero-sum games, for every $1\leq k\leq N^{1/2}$ the worst-case correlated-equilibrium gap achievable by a distribution supported on at most $k$ pure profiles is $$ Θ\left( \min\left\{1,\frac{\sqrt{\log N}}{k^{1/4}}\right\} \right), $$ which implies a $Θ(\log^2 N/\varepsilon^4)$ worst-case support bound. The proof builds on a probabilistic-method construction based on random sign matrices.

title_en: Canonical activation patterns and ReLU pattern varieties
abstract_en: A ReLU pattern variety records the polynomial relations among the coefficients of the affine maps associated with a prescribed set of activation patterns of a ReLU network. We study how the combinatorics of the canonical set of activation patterns of an unbiased ReLU network is reflected in the geometry of its pattern variety. title_en: Measuring Coherence in Predictive Models
abstract_en: Many sequential decision-making procedures, such as active learning, implicitly assume that a model's current predictions agree with those it expects to make after updating on new data, a property we call coherence. Most models in use do not update by exact conditioning and are not guaranteed to be coherent, which can lead to worse decisions. Yet there is currently no general way to measure incoherence or to tell when it matters. We develop tools to measure incoherence and characterise when it affects decisions. We introduce the incoherence ratio, an MMD-based measure of how far any updating procedure departs from coherence, computed only from the procedure's own predictions and updates, and accompany it with an anytime-valid test of coherence. In Bayesian experimental design, acquisition objectives that are equivalent for coherent models choose different data under every approximate model we study, and the incoherence ratio tracks how far incoherence distorts them. We also introduce action coherence, which captures only the incoherence that changes a decision. What a resulting disagreement costs, however, is determined primarily by predictive accuracy. Sequential decisions depend on how a model updates as well as on what it predicts, so coherence, like accuracy, should be checked rather than assumed.

title_en: The Manifold-Index Model: provably and efficiently avoiding the statistical and computational curse of dimensionality
abstract_en: We study vector-valued regression with predictors filling a tube around an unknown $m$-dimensional manifold $\mathcal{M}$ in $\mathbb{R}^D$. Multiscale ANisotropic lOcal Regression (MANOR) estimates tangent planes by multiscale PCA of predictors with similar responses, then refines them by pooling outer products of local slopes. The neighborhoods narrow tangentially while retaining complete normal fibers. We assume a Lipschitz link differential and bounded response noise. For $p\ge m$, under our geometric and sampling conditions, $n$ independent observations give mean tangent-space error of order $n^{-2/(m+4)}$ and integrated squared prediction error at the $m$-dimensional nonparametric rate $n^{-4/(m+4)}$, up to logarithmic factors. In a scaling regime with fixed intrinsic dimension, model and scale parameters, and ratio of manifold volume to the $m$-th power of its reach, the required sample size grows polynomially in $D+p$, and computation is polynomial in $n$, $D$ and $p$. The M-step remains in closed form, expectation maximization keeps its monotone ascent, and ML ($λ=0$) and the population model ($λ\to\infty$) are limiting cases. The prior strength was selected on 35 subjects of the PhysioNet EEG Motor Movement/Imagery Dataset and applied unchanged to 70 held-out subjects and to BCI Competition IV-2a. With $λ=1$ the held-out log-likelihood exceeded that of ML in 61 of 70 subjects (Holm-adjusted $p=9.1\times10^{-8}$) and in all 70 subjects with five training trials per class. A prior learned only from the PhysioNet data improved the held-out likelihood of all nine BCI IV-2a subjects at five trials per class and reduced the error of the joint transition matrix by 61%. Decoding accuracy did not improve ($p=0.17$). Cross-subject priors therefore stabilize few-trial dynamic models of motor-imagery EEG, but they do not improve decoding, which in these data relies mainly on structure shared across subjects.

title_en: Kernel-Guided Learning of Lifted Sparse Polynomial Models of Nonlinear Dynamical Systems
abstract_en: Polynomial models of dynamical systems enable constructive analysis via sum-of-squares programming. Yet, many physical systems involve non-polynomial nonlinearities which for certain classes of systems may be inferred from the underlying physics even when the exact dynamics are unknown. We show that fitting lifted polynomial models directly to lifted data is problematic, since the exact lifting constraints render the lifted derivatives linearly dependent. Instead, we learn the dynamics in the extended state, i.e., the state together with the known nonlinearities, and obtain the dynamics of the nonlinearities via the exact lifting relations. To avoid the combinatorially large libraries that sparse regression requires when the polynomial degrees are unknown, we propose KINDy, which selects the degree of each component by kernel ridge regression before applying sparse regression to the correspondingly reduced library. We prove that, for sufficiently small noise and regularization, provided the data satisfy a rank condition, the selected degree never underestimates the true degree. On the cart-pole system, KINDy recovers the true degrees at low noise levels and achieves speedups of up to 8.5 over sparse regression on the full library, while in almost all cases yielding models that are at least as sparse and have lower or equal test errors.

title_en: Locational Marginal Pricing of Compute: Co-optimizing Compute and Energy for Transparent Data Center Flexibility
abstract_en: Demand from data centers and AI compute is growing rapidly and is increasing stress on the power grid. This load could be flexible through user adjustments and provide relief during energy scarcity events, yet today its flexibility is provided through utility call-ups or system-operator load shedding, and is invisible to the users whose workloads are being curtailed. In this work, we propose to quantify and couple the prices of compute and energy in a single optimization problem. The resulting compute price reflects the marginal cost of the binding constraints and decomposes into components indicating which grid, power, hardware, or service requirement causes a price surge. The economic interpretation updates the price with real-time conditions and gives users a signal for potential flexibility provision. The co-optimization ultimately connects compute and energy markets while providing a signal for relief of stress on both the grid and the compute resources.

title_en: SAFER: Navigating the Exploration-Exploitation Dilemma in World-Model-Based Planning for Autonomous Driving
abstract_en: An autonomous vehicle must foresee the consequences of its actions, especially in the rare, time-critical situations where crashes happen. A world model offers this foresight, but only within the coverage of its training data, which poses an exploration-exploitation dilemma. Within this coverage a planner can hardly improve on the data, and beyond it the model's errors mislead it. Logs of competent driving rarely contain the failures that would widen the coverage, and agents that learn from interaction gain them only by failing themselves, without being shown what to do instead. We propose SAFER, a framework that learns offline from failures that others make, judged by an expert, and keeps learning online from its own driving. Offline, partially trained agents and scripted, recoverable perturbations Stage failures in simulation, and an expert Annotates every visited state with its action and value, so that much of what the planner explores is covered before it drives. In planning, a chunked latent world model Foresees the consequences fast enough for real-time use, and a risk-aware sampling-based planner Evaluates candidate maneuvers by their return minus a bounded collision penalty. Online, a loop continuously Refines the model wherever this driving leaves the coverage of the offline data. In closed-loop evaluation against the compared methods, SAFER reaches the highest route completion and reward per step on the CARLA Leaderboard routes, 0.95 and 0.77 from a privileged bird's-eye view, and the highest episode reward in MetaDrive, 53.4 in regular and 49.0 in safety-critical traffic. title_en: Washout-free synchronization, parameter estimation and uncertainty quantification of echo state networks
abstract_en: Echo state networks (ESNs) forecast chaotic systems for several Lyapunov times. Like all recurrent networks, ESNs require a washout before forecasting, i.e., a phase in which the full state drives the network until the reservoir state synchronizes with the system. At deployment, however, sensors measure only part of the state, with noise and at a lower sampling rate than the training data. We propose a washout-free deployment of ESNs via ensemble data assimilation. In closed loop, the ESN is a Markovian dynamical system; hence, a sequential filter can correct its reservoir state whenever data are available. The filter synchronizes an ensemble of reservoir states, drawn from the training data, with the system, and quantifies the forecast uncertainty. We extend the method to parametric ESNs, to infer physical parameters, and to parallel ESNs with localization, to forecast high-dimensional systems. We test the method on the Lorenz-63 and Lorenz-96 systems. First, the filter synchronizes the ESN with a fraction of the data of a washout. Second, the filter deploys one full-state ESN from a subset of its components, which a washout cannot do. Third, the filter estimates a forcing that is not in the training data, and the estimated forcing lengthens the forecast. Fourth, localization synchronizes a parallel ESN with eight times fewer members than the global filter. Fifth, the ensemble spread signals, without the true state, when the ESN synchronizes and when the filter fails. This work enables the deployment of ESNs from partial, sparse and noisy observations.

title_en: Does Learning Order Explain Forgetting? The Lie Bracket as an Early-Warning Signal for Catastrophic Forgetting Without Old Data
abstract_en: A network trained on task A and then task B ends at different weights than one trained on B and then A. To leading order this gap is set by the Lie bracket of the two tasks' gradient fields, and Dherin (2023) conjectured that a non-vanishing bracket may be linked to catastrophic forgetting. I test this conjecture empirically. Across Split MNIST, Split Fashion-MNIST and Split CIFAR-10, the forgetting of A is almost exactly the difference in A's loss between the two training orders (Spearman rho = 0.96-1.00). I then ask whether the bracket can predict that forgetting early in training on B and without any of A's data, using only a small summary stored when A finishes: its gradient and its top 20 Hessian eigenpairs. When the old task is well learned and forgetting is slow (task-incremental), this stored bracket ranks forgetting with rho = 0.70-0.81, against 0.33-0.58 for the penalty of Elastic Weight Consolidation, and matches or exceeds re-evaluating A on its own data. When forgetting is fast (domain-incremental), the stored summary goes stale and the EWC penalty is as good or better. The bracket fails outright when the old task is only half learned; I trace this to a residual gradient on A an order of magnitude larger, which makes first-order (slope) damage matter. The bracket is therefore a useful early-warning signal for the quiet kind of forgetting, under a clear condition.

title_en: Trading Parameters for Accuracy in MambaVision for Chest Radiograph Classification
abstract_en: MambaVision, a hybrid state-space and attention backbone, places most of its parameters in its widest, fourth stage. We quantified what that stage contributes to multi-label chest radiograph classification. The fourth stage was replaced with lighter single-scan state-space blocks adapted from Spatial-Mamba, with multi-scale dilated depthwise convolutions applied to the scan output; the first three stages were retained. Tiny, Small, and Base models were evaluated across nine dataset-scale combinations drawn from two source cohorts: the National Institutes of Health ChestX-ray14 archive (full ChestMNIST and a high-resolution subset) and Indiana University Open-i. At the Tiny scale, replacement reduced parameter count by 35.7% and increased graphics processing unit throughput by 19.3%; the savings came from the stage's dense projections, not from removing quadratic attention. Without distillation, the mean area under the receiver operating characteristic curve on ChestMNIST was 0.004 lower than the baseline (95% bootstrap confidence interval, 0.002 to 0.006), and 0.003 to 0.006 lower across all nine combinations. Knowledge distillation from an unreplaced teacher narrowed the gap to the undistilled baseline to 0.001-0.002 and met the equivalence criterion on ChestMNIST, but distilling the baseline with the same recipe improved it by 0.001-0.003, so a gap of 0.002-0.005 persisted under symmetric training. At the Base scale, the unreplaced Small model was both smaller and more accurate. Fourth-stage replacement is a useful trade-off only for Tiny and Small models. These measurements let developers of chest radiograph screening tools weigh model size and speed against a quantified loss of diagnostic discrimination.

title_en: Spatial phase coherence and its applications to masking and adaptive neighborhood sizing in multitemporal InSAR
abstract_en: We examine spatial phase coherence (SPC), a measure of the correlation between the wrapped phase time series of two pixels in a stack of single-look synthetic aperture radar acquisitions. A pixel and its adjacent neighbors share speckle through the point spread function, so that decorrelation alone does not lower their SPC below a floor. We find that masking pixels whose mean SPC to their eight neighbors is well below that floor, as in parts of layover and shadow areas, is an inexpensive complement to geometry-derived layover and shadow masks. For distributed scatterer pixels, averaging SPC over a fixed set of neighbors that share no speckle yields a proxy for the local coherence, the phase coherence indicator (PCI), that is available before the selection of statistically homogeneous pixels (SHPs). In phase estimation, averaging more pixels reduces noise but may also increase the bias in heterogeneous areas. To relax this trade-off, we propose to enhance SHP selection algorithms by scaling the search window size according to the PCI and truncating the set of selected pixels where a smaller nested set agrees clearly better with the phases at the center. In simulations of a TerraSAR-X and a Sentinel-1 stack with 44 and 79 acquisitions, we apply this adaptive neighborhood sizing (ANS) to established amplitude- and covariance-based SHP selection algorithms with thresholds that adapt to the PCI. Without ANS, the largest tested search window size has 13 to 29 % more phase linking error than the best of the tested sizes. With ANS, the largest window has the lowest error of the tested sizes, 11 % lower than that of the same selection at its best tested size without ANS. On a real TerraSAR-X stack, the mask based on SPC flags pixels in building shadows that a terrain model misses. On real Sentinel-1 stacks, ANS preserves dense fringes on a slowly deforming slope and in part on a fast landslide.

title_en: Mandarin Wh-Indefinites Follow Nonveridicality in Multilingual LLMs, Unlike English any
abstract_en: Multilingual LLMs learn mostly from English. Do they carry English polarity licensing over to other languages? English any is licensed by downward-entailing (DE) contexts, Mandarin wh-indefinites such as shenme 'what/something' by nonveridical ones, and the two classes come apart: perhaps licenses shenme but not any, while only licenses any but entails existence. We test this dissociation in a pre-registered study of twelve open LLMs (0.5B-9B, four families), using 48 matched bilingual frames in 21 contexts and a log-probability difference-in-differences normalised by negation. All 11 models that pass the measurement gate license Mandarin wh-indefinites under possibility, necessity and evidential adverbs, at 0.42-2.33 times the strength of negation, while English any gets nothing in the same contexts. An exploratory extension to Qwen2.5-32B shows the same. The English side is weaker: any under only, first and regret is licensed but at a fraction of negation, so only 3 models show the full double dissociation in sentence probabilities. When prompted to choose between sentences, most gated models show it. In exploratory directional ablations, a direction that carries English licensing, held-out classes included, does not reach Mandarin licensing in most models. The models do not simply apply the English rule to Mandarin.

title_en: Improving fine-grained expressivity of graph neural networks
abstract_en: This thesis investigates the expressive power of neural networks for structured data, focusing on graph neural networks and symmetry-aware architectures. We present four main contributions. First, we characterize the generic expressive power of geometric message-passing neural networks on sparse graphs and introduce EGenNet, an architecture achieving the corresponding guarantees. Second, we use representation theory to characterize linear layers equivariant to multiple permutations, including wreath-product symmetries. Third, we study permutation-invariant set representations that preserve containment, establish dimensional bounds and impossibility results, and introduce MASNet. Finally, we propose FSW-GNN, a message-passing architecture combining strong expressivity and bi-Lipschitz stability guarantees with strong empirical performance on long-range graph-learning tasks. Together, these results provide a broader understanding of how neural architectures can preserve the geometric, algebraic, order-theoretic, and metric structure of their inputs.

title_en: Kolmogorov-Arnold Lookup Table Demappers for Amplitude Phase-Shift Keying over Nonlinear Satellite Links
abstract_en: Next-generation high-throughput satellites increasingly demodulate and decode on board, so the per-symbol cost of the receiver constrains payload power and throughput. Soft demappers for nonlinear satellite links must therefore produce accurate bit log-likelihood ratios (LLRs) at low cost. We introduce a KAN-LUT demapper, a two-layer Kolmogorov--Arnold network (KAN) whose learned univariate edge functions are stored as 128-entry lookup tables (LUTs), so that inference needs only table reads, linear interpolation, and additions. We bound the LLR error introduced by the tables and evaluate the demapper on amplitude phase-shift keying (APSK) links with low-density parity-check (LDPC) coding and a nonlinear traveling-wave-tube amplifier. For 16-, 32-, and 64-APSK, KAN-LUT stays within 0.2 dB of a per-cluster Gaussian log-MAP (LogMAP-CG) demapper, while its cost relative to LogMAP-CG falls from 87% to 27% as the order grows. It matches or slightly exceeds multilayer perceptrons (MLPs) at about one fifth of their cost, remains competitive under operating-point mismatch, and needs only tens of kilobytes of tables. KAN-LUT is therefore a low-cost candidate demapper for regenerative payloads.

title_en: Communication-Efficient Distributionally Robust Federated Averaging with Multi-Source Data
abstract_en: Federated learning trains a shared model from distributed client data. The deployment risk is typically specified through two approximations: each unknown local distribution is replaced by its empirical distribution, and the unknown deployment mixture across clients is replaced by empirical or prescribed training weights. Existing robust methods usually address one approximation at a time through local distributional ambiguity sets or worst-case client mixtures. However, joint treatment of both approximations remains underexplored. To address this gap, we construct a global ambiguity set formed by admissible mixtures of client-wise Wasserstein ambiguity sets, yielding a distributionally robust optimization formulation. The construction allows client-dependent ambiguity radii, preserves client-wise separability of the objective function, and yields a high-probability out-of-sample guarantee for the resulting robust problem. We then introduce a penalty-based approximation of this formulation and develop a communication-efficient algorithm called BiDRO-FedAvg, for which we establish a convergence guarantee. We validate the proposed framework through a market-demand prediction simulation.

title_en: Weighted conformal prediction under covariate shift: process limits, estimated weights and efficiency
abstract_en: Weighted split conformal prediction handles covariate shift by reweighting calibration scores with the likelihood ratio $v=dQ_X/dP_X$; its training-conditional coverage is a functional of the self-normalized weighted empirical distribution function $\hat F_m$, and we study the process $\sqrt m(\hat F_m-F_Q)$. It converges in $\ell^\infty$ to the Gaussian process $W(G(t))-F_Q(t)W(K^2)$, with $G(t)=\mathbb{E}_Q[v\mathbf{1}\{S\le t\}]$ and $K^2=1+χ^2(Q\|P)$, if and only if $χ^2(Q\|P)<\infty$ (for non-degenerate scores); $\sup v$ plays no role. The limit gives the joint law of the coverage across levels, consistent bootstraps, inflations asymptotically exact uniformly in the level, and Berry-Esseen-type rates. With estimated ratios, a uniform expansion remains valid when the estimate uses the calibration covariates; the estimation error enters through a covariance term that can reduce the variance below the oracle's, and a pairs bootstrap reproduces it. When the ratio is known, the weighted conformal threshold is semiparametrically efficient if and only if the ratio and the coverage indicator are uncorrelated under the test distribution, with an explicit efficient correction otherwise. When $χ^2(Q\|P)=\infty$, the ratio has a regularly varying tail of index $p\in(1,2)$ and the score decouples from it in the far tail, the finite-dimensional limits are $p$-stable at the rate $m^{1-1/p}$ up to a slowly varying factor.

title_en: MOBO-CAPS: Multi-Objective Bayesian Optimization with Cardinality-Aware Pareto Selection
abstract_en: Multi-objective Bayesian optimization (MOBO) traditionally aims to approximate the entire Pareto front, but, due to resource constraints, real-world deployment is often limited to testing a small, representative subset of solutions. Hence current methods first approximate the full front before selecting solutions, potentially wasting costly evaluations. We formalize this problem as Multi-objective Bayesian Optimization with Cardinality-aware Pareto Selection (MOBO-CAPS), where the goal is to identify a set of exactly M solutions with high hypervolume. We propose two practical cardinality-aware acquisition strategies: REHVI, a replacement-aware approximation to expected hypervolume improvement, and CHO-UCB, which constructs an optimistic M-point set by optimizing a collective UCB-based hypervolume objective. We prove a sublinear simple regret bound for the batched version of CHO-UCB, and empirically show that cardinality-aware acquisition design improves over standard MOBO followed by post-hoc subset selection across nine benchmarks.

title_en: Value and Policy Calibration from Execution Feedback for Socially Compatible Driving
abstract_en: Autonomous vehicle (AV) decisions at intersections affect the delay, braking, and motion smoothness of surrounding human-driven vehicles (HDVs). Learning socially compatible behavior requires connecting imagined interaction outcomes with feedback from executed actions. We propose a world-model reinforcement learning framework combines imagined policy improvement with direct value and policy calibration from finalized interactions, balancing AV progress with HDV interaction burden. An interaction-aware latent model supports imagination, while off-policy correction and replay updates enable observed rewards and transitions to supervise both the critic and actor. Ablations identify complementary roles for value calibration in reducing HDV burden and policy calibration in improving passage efficiency. Tests under out-of-distribution traffic shifts further show lower ego jerk and HDV acceleration variation than PIWM at comparable passage times.

title_en: CoSyDelay: Cognitive Symbolic Regression for Traffic Delay Estimation
abstract_en: Trustworthy estimation of traffic delays at signalized intersections is critical for modern transportation systems, as it supports proactive traffic control for congestion mitigation. Existing analytical methods often rely on idealized assumptions that limit their accuracy under complex traffic conditions, whereas data-driven methods may achieve strong estimation performance but usually lack transparent structures, which reduces confidence in their practical application. To address these limitations, we propose CoSyDelay, a cognitive symbolic regression (SR) framework for automatically deriving explicit and physically consistent empirical delay estimation expressions (DEEs). Specifically, CoSyDelay decomposes intersection-level delay estimation into turning-movement-level subproblems, thereby reducing the complexity of the symbolic search. During DEE learning, CoSyDelay constructs domain-informed symbolic inputs from traffic variables. Large language models (LLMs) are employed as symbolic search operators to iteratively generate and refine candidate expression structures, whose movement-specific coefficients are subsequently calibrated using approach-level delay labels. A composite fitness function evaluates the learned DEEs jointly in terms of estimation accuracy and compliance with specified traffic-delay principles. Experimental results on multiple signalized intersections demonstrate that the resulting expressions achieve competitive estimation performance while maintaining physical consistency, thereby supporting trustworthy delay estimation. Source code and datasets are available at https://github.com/ForrestXie9/CoSyDelay.

title_en: Does synthetic pre-training pay off on a microcontroller? Accuracy, latency and energy across two MCUs
abstract_en: Rendered images are cheap to label, but a microcontroller classifier must survive 8-bit integer (INT8) quantisation and compute correctly on the chip. Five models, from MobileNetV2 at 224 px to a 61K-parameter convolutional neural network (CNN), were fine-tuned on a six-class scene dataset with and without a synthetic stage, against thresholds fixed in advance, and deployed on an ESP32-S3 and an RP2040. With full real data the stage gave no detectable gain. For the main deployable model the INT8 difference was +0.312 percentage points (pp), its interval below the +1.6 pp gain recomputed from the source study; quantisation did not detectably change it, nor did model size. With 10% of the real data the stage paid off for the CNN, by +3.438 pp on one seed and +2.715 pp over three; its cause is open. On the ESP32-S3 the main model took 152.7 ms and 16.3 mJ above idle per inference, and adding the stage changed neither beyond preset bounds. The model's INT8 outputs matched TensorFlow Lite's reference kernels exactly, but only after a memory overrun in a vendor kernel was patched. On the RP2040 the same model took 1.80 s and 27.3 mJ above idle, about twelve times slower, and the largest 96 px model exceeded the board's flash-capacity limit. Neither the RP2040 nor the host interpreter used for scoring reproduced the reference arithmetic. A synthetic stage is worth adding only when real data are scarce, and on-device INT8 outputs should be checked against reference kernels, not inferred from host scores.

title_en: Delayed Heuristic-Behavior-Target Coupling for Off-Policy Reinforcement Learning in Inventory Control
abstract_en: Many reinforcement learning methods tie data collection to the task policy, while coordinating independently optimized behavior and target policies remains challenging. Policies learned by these methods can perform unreliably in long-horizon tasks under uncertainty, such as inventory control, where failures can incur extreme costs. Generation-level diagnostics trace heuristic uptake and subsequent selective target responses, while component ablations support the contribution of this transmission mechanism to policy recovery and improvement.

title_en: Dynamic Spatio-Temporal Graph Attention Networks with Nested Clustered Optimization for Multi-Asset Portfolios
abstract_en: Nested Clustered Optimization (NCO) insulates asset allocation from Markowitz covariance ill-conditioning. However, classical tree clustering relies on static pairwise Pearson correlation, failing to capture time-varying, asymmetric downside risk contagion across multi-asset markets. We propose a unified deep graph machine learning architecture: Dynamic Spatio-Temporal Graph Attention Networks with Nested Clustered Optimization (ST-GAT-NCO) for multi-asset tactical allocation. The framework extracts temporal momentum and downside risk dynamics via causal dilated 1D-convolutions, then deploys a multi-head Graph Attention Network (GAT) over dynamic market topologies to learn latent spatial node representations. These learned embeddings define an angular metric distance space that guides two-stage downside NCO optimization under institutional constraints and turnover smoothing. Evaluated over a 73-month non-anticipative walk-forward out-of-sample window (January 2020 to January 2026) across 13 global asset classes net of 10 bps transaction costs, ST-GAT-NCO achieves a 5.32% CAGR and 37.06% cumulative net return, delivering an excess Sharpe ratio of 0.30 and a Sortino ratio of 0.48. This substantially outperforms classical Minimum Variance (3.68% CAGR, 0.08 Sharpe), Hierarchical Risk Parity (2.65% CAGR), and Plain Symmetric NCO (4.11% CAGR, 0.15 Sharpe), while restricting maximum drawdown to -13.07% (versus -19.44% for Equal-Weight and -16.36% for Downside NCO) under a controlled one-way turnover of 15.31%/month. Regime analysis confirms active capital preservation across the 2020 COVID-19 crash, 2022 monetary tightening, and 2023-2026 disinflation rallies.

title_en: First-order smoothed exact-penalty methods for equality-constrained regularized nonconvex optimization
abstract_en: We consider regularized nonconvex optimization over a closed convex set $\mathcal{X} \subseteq \mathbb{R}^d$, which involves a convex nonsmooth regularizer $r$ in the objective and $n$ smooth equality constraints. To find a near-KKT point of the problem, we propose a prox-linear first-order method, named as SEPi-Prox, based on a smoothed exact-penalty formulation. At each outer iteration of SEPi-Prox, a strongly convex prox-linear subproblem is formed and solved inexactly to a sufficient accuracy. Under a local non-singularity condition that is weaker than some other commonly used regularity conditions or constraint qualifications, SEPi-Prox finds an $ε$-KKT point within $O(ε^{-2})$ first-order oracle calls, matching the lower bound for unconstrained smooth nonconvex optimization. We employ Nesterov's accelerated proximal-gradient method (APG) and a dual cutting-plane method (DCP) for the prox-linear subproblems. Let $\mathcal{C}_{\mathrm{FO}}$ and $\mathcal{C}_r$ denote the numbers of arithmetic operations of evaluating one first-order oracle and one proximal mapping of $r$ over $\mathcal{X}$, respectively. Then SEPi-Prox requires $\widetilde{O}(\mathcal{C}_{\mathrm{FO}}ε^{-2} + (dn + \mathcal{C}_r)ε^{-5/2})$ and $\widetilde{O}((\mathcal{C}_{\mathrm{FO}} + dn^2 + n\mathcal{C}_r + n^{3.373})ε^{-2})$ total arithmetic operations to produce an $ε$-KKT point, respectively by using APG and DCP as the subsolver. The latter result is preferable when $n$ is small and nearly matches the optimal dependence on $ε$. Numerical experiments on instances of the multi-class Neyman-Pearson classification demonstrate the efficiency of SEPi-Prox with both subsolvers.

title_en: Wideband Hybrid Beamforming via Programmable Unitary Mixer--TTD RF Networks
abstract_en: This paper proposes a wideband hybrid beamforming architecture whose analog front-end consists of fixed unitary mixers interlaced with programmable diagonal phase-shift/true-time-delay (TTD) layers. title_en: Local Order Matters: A Lightweight CPU-Trainable CNN for Website Fingerprinting on Defended Tor Traffic
abstract_en: Website fingerprinting (WF) attacks let a passive adversary infer which site a Tor user visits from the encrypted cell sequence. title_en: Max-Min Throughput in RSMA-Aided SWIPT for Sustainable Internet of Underground Things: A Deep Reinforcement Learning Approach

title_en: Certified Algorithms for Gaussian Location Mixture NPMLEs via Discretized Gradient Flows
abstract_en: We study the computation of approximate nonparametric maximum likelihood estimators (NPMLEs) for Gaussian location mixtures in arbitrary dimension $d\ge 1$ via the Fisher-Rao gradient flow. En route, we also establish results on the well-posedness and convergence properties of the continuous-time Fisher--Rao flow. title_en: NoLBERT-Calls: Reading Earnings Calls Without Hindsight
abstract_en: Language models are now a standard tool for measuring what managers say on earnings calls, but the encoders behind these measures were usually pretrained on text from the same years a backtest covers. Holding out a test period does not remove that hindsight, because it sits in the features. We adapt NoLBERT, an encoder pretrained only on text published between 1976 and 1995, to earnings calls without letting it read anything dated after 31 December 2023. The calls supply the training signal themselves: every analyst question is followed by management's answer, and the model learns to pick that answer out from the other answers of the same call. We test on every US call from January 2025 to October 2026 (20,323 calls, 254,575 questions) and make every modeling choice on calls from 2024. The adapted model, NoLBERT-Calls-2023, ranks the true answer first for 78.0% of questions (95% interval 77.8-78.2; chance 8.0%), against 26.3% before adaptation. It is 1.0 point ahead of a call-adapted ChronoBERT, 3.4 points ahead of a call-adapted FinBERT, and 18.7 and 19.8 points ahead of the best off-the-shelf retriever and BM25. A year-by-year test over 2013-2026 finds no look-ahead premium: relative to a model adapted only through 2012, the released model does no better on the years it was trained on than on years it never saw. The price of the cutoff is compute: under one shared 150-minute recipe NoLBERT adapts least well of four encoders, and its lead comes from a longer, staged adaptation of about 13 GPU-hours.

title_en: Sharp Gaussian Approximation for Q-Learning
abstract_en: Gaussian approximation provides a foundation for online statistical inference in reinforcement learning. We establish sharp non-asymptotic Gaussian approximation rates in Wasserstein distance for asynchronous Q-learning with Polyak-Ruppert averaging. We prove an upper bound of $\widetilde{O}(n^{-1/4})$, where $n$ is the number of iterations, together with a matching lower bound up to logarithmic factors. Q-learning is more challenging to analyze than linear stochastic approximation due to the nonlinearity of the Bellman operator. Asynchronous updates introduce further challenges due to Markovian noise. Our analysis separates the errors from Bellman nonlinearity, Markovian noise, and the finite-sample covariance discrepancy. In particular, we show that Markovian noise induces an unavoidable bias even when the Bellman operator is linear. The trade-off between this bias and the covariance discrepancy determines the convergence rate. We further extend our analysis to the synchronous setting and establish a sharp rate of $\widetilde{O}(n^{-1/2})$.

title_en: How Should Parallel Langevin Chains Share Noise?
abstract_en: Parallel Langevin sampling usually draws an array of independent Gaussian vectors, one row per chain. The average row drives the ensemble mean, with variance $1/K$ per coordinate for $K$ chains. Yet the unadjusted Langevin algorithm (ULA) specifies only each row's distribution. Subtracting the column means and rescaling, as in classical antithetic sampling, makes that variance zero. Each chain keeps its ordinary ULA path law for any finite run. For quadratic targets we derive the joint covariance of linear estimates computed from the ensemble mean, including coefficient estimates, time averages and predictions. The identity separates contributions from initial states and Gaussian draws. The coupling changes the second through one scalar, which is zero whenever the draws sum to zero across chains. For nonquadratic targets we bound the remaining variance. Centering has a price: for a quadratic form in the mean-subtracted Gaussian state, the ensemble average has variance $1/(K-1)$ relative to one chain, compared with $1/K$ under independent draws. On three tempered logistic posteriors, eight centered chains reduced the variance of the posterior-mean estimate, summed over coordinates, by two to three orders of magnitude compared with eight independent chains. They also beat 128 independent chains on variance and on variance times sampling time. Under Metropolis correction the reduction shrank to about three- to eightfold: rejected draws no longer balance accepted ones. The measured variance ratios were consistent with a leading-order prediction from rejection frequency and noise energy.

title_en: Ambiguous Examples Help, But Full Data Wins: Revisiting Dataset Cartography for Extractive Adversarial QA
abstract_en: Dataset cartography argues that training dynamics can reveal regions of a dataset that matter differently for learning: easy-to-learn examples aid optimization, hard-to-learn examples often expose annotation problems, and ambiguous examples contribute strongly to out-of-distribution generalization. Ambiguous-ranked 33% subsets beat random 33% subsets on exact-match accuracy in all 14 model-evaluation cells and on F1 in 12/14 cells. However, full-data training beats ambiguous-ranked training in 12/14 exact-match cells and 12/14 F1 cells, with mean full-minus-ambiguous gains of 3.40 EM and 4.10 F1. The most thoroughly replicated ELECTRA-small panel is also the main exception to the ambiguous-over-random F1 gains. title_en: Cache or Denoise Less? Residual Reuse in a Flow-Matching World Action Model
abstract_en: Flow-matching robot policies generate each action chunk through repeated network evaluations, one per denoising step. Cross-cycle caches such as C$^3$ache reuse computation from earlier replanning calls, but whether they beat simply taking fewer steps is unclear. A cache that keeps two fresh steps cannot be faster than two uncached steps: every call still encodes the images, runs the video expert and computes those two steps. Caching the first of two steps, refreshed every fourth call, saves at most 11--14% of a call by our cost model. Cached policies are also fragile. Their losses tracked the share of the flow path the cached steps cover: under Fast-WAM's current time shift, C$^3$ache's eight cached steps cover 80% of the path instead of 44%, and the cached policy succeeds on 63% of states against 95% uncached. title_en: Architecting the Corporate AI Infrastructure: The Evolving Roles of AI Governance Committees and Chief Ethics Officers
abstract_en: The accelerating integration of artificial intelligence (AI) into core business operations has created an urgent need for robust corporate governance infrastructures capable of managing complex ethical, legal, and operational risks. title_en: RIFT: Reward Improvement Field Transfer for Cross-Domain Offline RL
abstract_en: Learning from limited target data is a central challenge in cross-domain offline reinforcement learning. Abundant source data can help, but dynamics differences can make direct transition reuse unreliable. It applies this field to low-reward target anchors and decodes the results to augment the target dataset. title_en: Mesoscale Neural Operators: Learning Nonlinear Constitutive Laws from Molecular Dynamics for Scalable Fracture Predictions
abstract_en: Molecular dynamics (MD) simulations can capture the nanoscale physics of fracture at the atomistic level, but their computational cost prohibits predictions at the length scales and time scales needed for many applications. Machine learning approaches, on the other hand, have been proposed as heuristic surrogates for material fracture, yet they cannot guarantee the physical consistency of the predicted response. To address this shortcoming, we propose the mesoscale neural operator (MNO): a data-driven nonlocal constitutive model that is learned directly from MD loading and displacement data. After training, it can be used in continuum fracture simulations on much larger domains and grid sizes. The key idea of the MNO is to exploit the built-in characteristic length of a nonlocal model, called the horizon, to travel across scales. Physical consistency across scales is obtained by building two structural ingredients into the MNO: a normalized kernel that renders the strain energy density invariant under horizon rescaling, and a rescaled critical bond stretch that keeps the energy release rate consistent across scales. Through tests on synthetic data, we show that the MNO and its learning workflow indeed discover the nonlocal continuum multiscale model in the form of the nonlocal kernel and the nonlinear constitutive relation. We then apply the framework to coarse-grained MD data and find that in a test problem, the learned model matches the MD strain energy density and critical energy release rate within 3%. It also predicts the peak transmitted forces within 6% in out-of-distribution tension tests. As a further demonstration, the model is applied to a plate with 4000 times the area of the training specimens and containing an initial defect. In this problem, the model reproduces the main features of dynamic brittle fracture, including branch and cascading branch networks.

title_en: BadGCL: Towards Persistent Backdoor Attack on Graph Continual Learning Systems
abstract_en: Backdoor attacks pose a persistent security threat to machine learning systems, yet their behavior under graph continual learning (GCL) remains underexplored. Conventional graph backdoor attacks often lose effectiveness as models are updated across successive tasks, creating the impression that continual updates naturally weaken malicious associations. This work reveals a contrasting vulnerability: knowledge-preservation mechanisms in GCL can also preserve early injected backdoors when the poisoned update is compatible with the clean-task signal being retained. For graph data, this risk is amplified by structural triggers, which are embedded into the message-passing paths of graph neural networks (GNNs) and can induce stable representation shifts across tasks. To expose this risk, we propose BadGCL, a model-agnostic framework for persistent backdoor attacks under a strict early-stage intervention setting. BadGCL learns topology-aware structural triggers using a gradient mutual-information objective that couples poisoned gradients with clean-task optimization signals, together with a propagation consistency objective that stabilizes trigger-induced effects through graph message passing. We provide theoretical analysis showing that gradient compatibility and propagation stability jointly support long-term backdoor persistence under benign continual updates. Extensive experiments across task-IL and class-IL protocols, four GCL benchmarks, and diverse victim systems show that BadGCL achieves persistent attack effectiveness with limited clean-utility degradation, substantially outperforming graph and continual-learning backdoor baselines and remaining robust against representative defenses.

title_en: NAP-Wave: A Neural Adaptive Plane-Wave Architecture for High-Frequency Helmholtz Problems
abstract_en: Training neural networks to simulate highly oscillatory wavefields presents optimization challenges, often hindered by spectral bias and poorly conditioned physics-based loss landscapes. To address these challenges and enhance convergence, we propose NAP-Wave, a joint neural architecture and training strategy that expands the target scattered wavefield in an adaptive neural plane-wave basis. The basis functions are extracted from all hidden layers and modulated by trainable plane-wave carriers, embedding the high-frequency oscillatory physics directly into the network's trial space. At each growth step, we avoid the loss spikes typical of dynamic network growth using the LS-computed coefficients, the warm-started parameters, and the preservation of the first- and second-order optimizer moments of the previous stage. Ablation studies confirm that the plane-wave basis, the exact coefficient solve, and the progressive schedule independently accelerate convergence and improve accuracy. Validated on exact-solution benchmarks, NAP-Wave achieves relative L2 errors of order 1%. On highly heterogeneous geophysical benchmarks, it achieves relative errors of 5%, 9%, and 10%, significantly outperforming published PINN methods in both accuracy and convergence time. title_en: Risk-Averse Decision-Focused Learning: Minimizing CVaR of Regret
abstract_en: Many combinatorial optimization (CO) problems involve parameters that are uncertain when the problem must be solved. In such settings, the parameters have to be predicted from correlated contextual information before a solution can be computed. \emph{Decision-focused learning} (DFL) addresses this by training the predictive model to produce predictions that optimize downstream decision quality. Most existing DFL methods are risk-neutral and minimize the expected regret. In high-stakes applications this can lead to undesirable outcomes, because decision-makers must also account for the tail risk of decision quality. Prior risk-sensitive approaches typically model uncertainty explicitly and solve a stochastic or robust optimization problem at inference time, which increases computational complexity. title_en: Learning from Mutants: Teaching Small Language Models to Synthesise Loop Invariants
abstract_en: Large language models (LLMs) have proven promising for synthesising loop invariants, a long-standing obstacle to automated program verification. Yet, frontier LLMs are typically accessible only through third-party APIs, hampering reproducibility and local deployment. Inspired by mutation testing, our approach applies semantic mutation operators to ground-truth invariants, producing semantic mutants that induce verification failure. Each mutant is paired with verifier feedback and its ground-truth counterpart, yielding training examples for feedback-guided invariant refinement. Whereas the vast space of mutants is a long-standing burden in mutation testing, it becomes an asset when generating training data, multiplying the examples obtainable from a fixed set of verified programs. title_en: SLiDE: Structured Linear Dynamics for Forecasting with Exogenous Inputs
abstract_en: Accurate time series forecasting with exogenous inputs is critical across domains, including energy and retail, yet modern deep learning models often overfit to correlations that do not generalize under shifts in these inputs. We propose SLiDE, a Koopman-inspired architecture for forecasting with exogenous inputs that imposes structure on latent temporal dynamics. SLiDE approximates nonlinear system evolution using a learned linear operator in a latent space, combining (i) a history encoder that reconstructs the current latent state from past targets and inputs with (ii) a shared linear rollout driven by future exogenous variables. By enforcing a common linear recurrence across encoding and prediction, SLiDE aligns how past information is encoded with how future states evolve, reducing parameterization and preventing reliance on spurious correlations in the input history. Empirically, SLiDE achieves state-of-the-art accuracy on real-world benchmarks, including electricity price forecasting and retail demand, while maintaining a computational footprint comparable to lightweight MLP architectures. SLiDE is especially effective at generalizing to shifted exogenous inputs, reducing MSE by 20% on electricity price samples with out-of-range exogenous values and MAE by 30% in a synthetic transfer setting where the same dynamical system is driven by an unseen exogenous process. Ablations confirm the importance of both the structured history encoder and the linear latent rollout, suggesting that structured latent linear dynamics provide a useful inductive bias for forecasting with exogenous inputs.

title_en: Bellman Residual Bracketing: Resolving the Sample Complexity of Discounted and Average-Reward RL
abstract_en: We study the sample complexity of the empirical planning or plug-in approach for reinforcement learning (RL) with a generative model. title_en: Sharp First-Hit Identification from Finite Depth Samples
abstract_en: Which depths in a new camera view are determined by finitely many source-depth measurements? Pointwise uncertainty bounds do not answer this question: unobserved geometry between samples can change which surface is encountered first. We study a bounded Lipschitz class of continuous source inverse-depth fields with interval observations and known camera pose. Building on classical Lipschitz envelopes, we characterize the exact set of attainable first-hit depths and construct a globally admissible scene for every value in that set. The set can be disconnected. We also give a necessary and sufficient test for several proposed depths to be first hits of one shared scene. An epipolar reduction uses scalar cone inequalities without enumerating surfaces. In a rectified model with source spacing $h$, interval half-width $\varepsilon$, baseline $b$, and slope bound $L$, we prove a sharp worst-case inverse-depth diameter of $\max\{Lh+2\varepsilon,2\varepsilon/(1-bL)\}$ when $bL<1$, subject to sufficient depth and domain range for attainment. Exact samples still give the sharp bound $Lh$ at $bL=1$, while above this threshold ambiguity need not vanish as sampling becomes arbitrarily dense. Any positive measurement uncertainty can destroy uniform stability at the critical threshold. We provide constructive examples, an exact rational validation oracle, and a frozen ten-scene evaluation using reference, stereo, and learned-depth observations. The experiments separate solver correctness under the scene assumptions from failure of those assumptions: fixed learned-depth bands often yield narrow but incorrect sets. The results identify what a specified scene class permits; they do not infer a continuum regularity or physical-scene guarantee from sampled predictions.

title_en: Steering Bayesian Inference and Decisions through Data Poisoning
abstract_en: Adversarial machine learning has revealed that statistical models can be manipulated through poisoned data, and Bayesian inference is no exception. Earlier work has shown that subtle poisoning attacks can drive the posterior toward a distribution of the attacker's choosing. Such posterior attraction attacks require a fully specified target posterior; however, attackers typically care about only a few posterior quantities or, more consequentially, about a downstream decision. Herein, we study how an attacker can alter Bayesian inference and decisions by deleting or replicating a few observations, chosen to minimize the maximum mean discrepancy between the resulting posterior and a target distribution. A suitable kernel lets the attacker steer selected posterior moments without specifying the rest of the target. Because Bayes actions depend on the posterior only through expected utilities, which are themselves posterior moments, the same approach can target a decision directly. We construct the attacks with a gradient-based heuristic that requires only posterior samples, and analyze its convergence. Experiments with regression and hierarchical models compare moment-based and full-posterior attacks, and illustrate how deleting a handful of observations can flip a Bayesian decision.

title_en: Formalizing Formal Semantics: The Formal Atlas
abstract_en: In this paper we present the Formal Atlas, a system for the study of natural language semantics using proof assistants. title_en: Geometric Stability and Sample Complexity for Compositional Function Priors
abstract_en: We study when compositional structure yields dimension reduction in supervised learning. We frame learning as empirical risk minimization with a function-space prior: a regularization functional selects a subset of functions with favorable approximation and metric entropy. The models are compositions $f(x)=g(Ax+Δh(x))$, where $A\in\mathbb{R}^{k\times d}$ is a linear base map, $Δh$ is a nonlinear correction, and $g$ is an outer function; that is, $f$ is an arbitrary smooth function of a $k$-dimensional representation of the input that is linear up to a correction. We prove covering-number bounds showing that the statistical complexity of this class interpolates between an intrinsic regime, parametric in the $kd$ entries of the linear map and nonparametric only in the representation dimension $k$, and an ambient $d$-dimensional nonparametric rate; the interpolation is controlled by the correction size $\varepsilon=\|Δh\|$. We then connect $\varepsilon$ to data geometry. If the data lie in a small tube around a $k$-dimensional manifold and the regression target depends on the input only through its nearest point on that manifold, then locally the target factorizes exactly as $g(Ax+Δh(x))$ with $A$ a tangent chart and a correction whose Sobolev norm scales linearly with curvature at the localization scale. Patching such local models over an atlas gives a finite-sample excess-risk bound for a least-squares estimator over a finite net of local models, whose ambient term vanishes with curvature. For a one-dimensional model problem we also prove a converse: on curved data, every affine compositional predictor faces an error floor unless its correction budget scales with curvature, while the matching curved model class attains the intrinsic rate. The correction size $\varepsilon$ is thus the effective-dimension parameter linking curvature to statistical complexity.

title_en: Probing SAM Perturbations Through Statistical Replay
abstract_en: Sharpness Aware Minimization (SAM) updates model parameters using gradients evaluated at adversarially perturbed weights, but it remains unclear which aspects of this procedure are sufficient to reproduce its generalization behavior. In our ResNet 18 experiments on CIFAR 10, simple curvature regularizers based on the Hessian trace and largest eigenvalue remain below SAM in validation accuracy, motivating a direct examination of its perturbations. We introduce statistical replay, a diagnostic that summarizes perturbations from reference SAM trajectories using elementwise means and standard deviations over local windows and constructs new perturbations during independent SGD training. Pure replay uses only these summaries, whereas mixed replay adds isotropic Gaussian noise. Pure replay does not reproduce SAM's validation behavior, while mixed replay and pure isotropic perturbations can approach its validation performance at selected scales without reproducing its training dynamics. An equal radius random direction within SAM performs similarly to SGD, and source, temporal, and layer interventions further suggest that replay behavior depends on perturbation construction. Together, these preliminary results weaken several simple explanations of SAM while leaving an important part of its mechanism unexplained.

title_en: Grokking Can Be Steered: Selecting Desirable Solutions By Choice Of Learning Rule
abstract_en: During grokking, a network transitions from memorization to generalization, yet what shapes the neural implementation (circuit) of the generalizing solution and specifically the number of participating neurons (its size) remains unclear. We find that the learning rule, the combination of credit assignment algorithm and optimizer, controls this: On modular addition, every learning rule we study that groks recovers the same Fourier-based algorithm, yet implemented by circuits that differ in size. Why? A neuron stays in use when its credit is large relative to the non-gradient term of its own update, and this single condition unifies three routes to unused neurons: the coupled weight decay, Adam's $ε$ and the decay of a trainable per-neuron gain. Equalizing the magnitude of credit assigned to each neuron, or scaling each neuron's weight decay by its credit, expands the effective circuit size, measured from the outgoing weights, from 60% to 99% of the layer's neurons at similar training and test accuracy. We vary which neurons share one equalization factor, from the whole layer to individual neurons, and find that the circuit stays concentrated for groups of eight or more and fully distributes only when every neuron has its own factor. Credit magnitudes are usually set by the normalization of standard optimizers: Nero, which normalizes per neuron, distributes the computation, whereas Adam and seven others, including RMSProp, Muon, and Shampoo, use other normalization schemes and retain small, concentrated circuits. Distributed circuits tolerate neuron deletion better, while concentrated circuits can be pruned further and transfer about twice as fast to a task that recombines the same features, largely by recruiting their unused neurons. Learning rule choice thus steers circuit size, trading robustness against compressibility and transfer speed without changing the learned algorithm.

title_en: Predicting, Fast and Slow: SSD Already Knows Which Guess Is Wrong
abstract_en: Heimdall, a learned controller, calls slow on 52% of an SSD's reads when 30% are slow. Uncertainty estimators, the remedy prescribed for its wrong guesses, cannot find them: nine of them do no better than a coin. The drive can. On one trace, 2% of the reads of 4 to 8 KiB that found less than 4 KiB outstanding while the drive was answering came back slow, and Heimdall called 96% of them slow. A 4,096-entry table of how the drive's recent reads came back, untrained and 21 ns a decision, ranks the wrong guesses at a median AUROC of 0.68 on 57 held-out traces, where the nine sit at 0.46 to 0.52, and it predicts slow reads better than Heimdall itself.

title_en: From Facts to Personas: Interpretable Role Unlearning in LLMs via Mixture-of-Experts
abstract_en: LLMs are widely adopted in multi-role dialogue and persona simulation. However, their strong ability to imitate role-specific linguistic and behavioral patterns can introduce privacy risks, reinforce social biases, and lead to unsafe or uncontrollable outputs. To address these issues, we introduce the Role-playing Unlearning task, which aims to selectively forget the style and knowledge associated with target roles while preserving the language ability and behaviors of the remaining roles. Unlike prior unlearning tasks that focus solely on removing factual information, our task additionally requires forgetting persona-specific characteristics, making the control over model generation more fine-grained. We propose RoleMoE, a Mixture-of-Experts framework that maps different roles to more independent expert subspaces, improving role separation and structural interpretability. To further distinguish role-specific features, RoleMoE incorporates two complementary losses: a specialization loss that drives roles to adopt distinct expert distributions, and a disentanglement loss that encourages experts to develop distinct capability subspaces. This decomposed structure enables role unlearning to focus selectively on target-role experts. We finally propose RoleBench-Unlearn for evaluation, and experiments on multiple backbone LLMs show that RoleMoE enables precise and controllable role forgetting, while better preserving the linguistic quality, knowledge, and persona consistency of non-target roles. All code and datasets are publicly available at: https://github.com/mbzuai-nlp/ROLEMOE.

title_en: Federated versus Centralized PV Capacity-Factor Forecasting: A Non-Inferiority Study Across Seven Stations in North Macedonia
abstract_en: Background: Photovoltaic (PV) forecasts inform energy commitments by PV operators and aggregators and guide charge-discharge scheduling in solar-plus-storage systems. title_en: DyTransRM: A Unified Simulation-to-Real Framework for Dynamic Radio Map Prediction
abstract_en: Dynamic radio map (RM) prediction enables proactive wireless network control by forecasting future propagation conditions from historical observations. title_en: Generalization Bounds for Neural Networks with Sparse Connectivity
abstract_en: Empirical evidence suggests that large neural networks rarely make effective use of all available parameters, with learned solutions exhibiting pronounced sparsity. Despite this ubiquity, existing generalization theory only partially explains how such sparsity influences statistical performance. In this paper, we derive non-asymptotic generalization gap bounds for deep neural networks whose layer-wise weight matrices are restricted by $\ell_p$ quasi-norm ($0<p\leq 1$) constraints. Our analysis gives rise to a novel result that interpolates between classical norm-based generalization guarantees and parameter-counting bounds. Remarkably, in the extreme sparsity limit as the quasi-norm order $p$ approaches zero, our analysis reveals a transition to a square-root dependence on the number of \emph{active} (non-zero) parameters, resulting in bounds that are strictly tighter than existing parameter-counting approaches. Experiments demonstrate that our bounds exhibit a milder dependence on initial architectural choice at the over-parametrization regime, effectively capturing the generalization benefit of the sparsity arising from training on natural data.
